policy.opposition: Retrieve only reviewed proposition-linked stances. A tradition label, geography, or entity name never creates an opposition relationship.
policy.comparison: Filter every evidence section before applying limits. Similarity never implies influence; only a cited, explicit influence relationship may be labeled influence.
policy.chronology: Retain ranges, date confidence, unknown dates, and survival-bias warnings. Earlier surviving evidence does not prove earliest origin.
policy.teachingConduct: Cite teaching and conduct independently, name actors and mixed motives, preserve evidence gaps, and never convert conduct into doctrine or issue a theological verdict.

propositions.title: Response to enemies
propositions.proposition: A person should answer hostility with love or non-retaliation.

propositions.title: A self survives death
propositions.proposition: A persisting self or person survives bodily death.

propositions.title: Suffering and providence
propositions.proposition: The extent of suffering counts against a perfectly good and powerful providence.

propositions.title: Religious coercion
propositions.proposition: Political authority may compel religious affiliation for institutional ends.

oppositionStances.title: Love and pray for enemies
oppositionStances.summary: Matthew 5:44–45 commands love and prayer for enemies in a particular Matthean teaching context.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Jesus as represented by the Gospel of Matthew
oppositionStances.historicalContext: First-century Christian gospel tradition; Atlas cites a historical English translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Translation and the relation of this passage to other New Testament violence texts require separate analysis.

oppositionStances.title: Hatred does not cease by hatred
oppositionStances.summary: Dhammapada verse 5 frames non-hatred as the means by which hatred ceases.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Pali Buddhist verse collection; the bundled Müller translation is historically situated.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: This maxim does not settle every Buddhist account of force, punishment, or governance.

oppositionStances.title: Recompense injury with justice
oppositionStances.summary: Analects 14.34 distinguishes a just response to injury from repaying virtue with virtue.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Confucius as represented in the Analects
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Received Confucian dialogue collection; translation of de and zhi affects nuance.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Justice need not entail revenge, so this is a qualification rather than a simple inversion.

oppositionStances.title: Recompense injury with kindness
oppositionStances.summary: The received Tao Te Ching chapter 63 is translated by Legge as recompensing injury with kindness.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Voice of the Tao Te Ching
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Received Chinese text in a nineteenth-century English translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The translation and textual history of the phrase are contested; no influence on Matthew is asserted.

oppositionStances.title: Vengeance rather than turning the other cheek
oppositionStances.summary: The Church of Satan's fifth statement explicitly presents vengeance as an alternative to turning the other cheek.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: A 1969 LaVeyan formulation reproduced by its official organization.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: This is one organization and one Satanic current; it cannot stand for all Satanists.

oppositionStances.title: Human welfare and reciprocal responsibility
oppositionStances.summary: Humanist Manifesto III grounds ethics in welfare and responsibility rather than a supernatural command to love enemies.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Modern organizational statement issued in 2003.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The manifesto does not directly adjudicate every response to attack; this is a bounded qualification.
oppositionStances.locator: Humanist Manifesto III, ethical-values and responsibility paragraphs

oppositionStances.title: Birthless and deathless self
oppositionStances.summary: The Bhagavad Gita describes the enduring self as not born and not dying, within Krishna's counsel to Arjuna.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Krishna as represented in the Bhagavad Gita
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Sanskrit epic dialogue in a historical poetic English translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Ātman, person, and modern English 'self' are not automatically equivalent.

oppositionStances.title: Resurrection rather than bare soul survival
oppositionStances.summary: John 5:28–29 depicts people in graves coming forth; this differs from a simple disembodied-soul claim.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Jesus as represented by the Gospel of John
oppositionStances.historicalContext: First-century Christian gospel tradition in a historical translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Resurrection and immortal-soul models must remain distinct even when both affirm postmortem life.

oppositionStances.title: The dead know nothing
oppositionStances.summary: Ecclesiastes 9:5 says the dead know nothing within a wisdom discourse about life under the sun.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: A biblical wisdom voice often placed in tension with later resurrection readings.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Scope ('under the sun') and canonical harmonization are disputed; this is not a summary of Judaism.

oppositionStances.title: Mind and soul are mortal
oppositionStances.summary: Lucretius' Epicurean poem argues that mind and soul are bodily and dissolve rather than persist after death.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: First-century BCE Roman Epicurean philosophical poetry.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: A poetic philosophical argument is not empirical proof of every modern materialist account.
oppositionStances.locator: On the Nature of Things, Book III, mortality-of-mind argument

oppositionStances.title: Personal-identity objections
oppositionStances.summary: Contemporary philosophy distinguishes bodily, psychological, resurrection, and soul-based criteria, with objections to each.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Contemporary peer-reviewed philosophical overview.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The field has no single consensus model of postmortem identity.
oppositionStances.locator: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Afterlife, sections 2–4

oppositionStances.title: Life accepted without supernaturalism
oppositionStances.summary: Humanist Manifesto III treats nature as self-existing and this life as enough without affirming supernatural survival.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Modern organizational statement, not all secular persons.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Absence of affirmation is not a scientific demonstration that survival is impossible.
oppositionStances.locator: Humanist Manifesto III, naturalism and life's fulfillment paragraphs

oppositionStances.title: Philo's challenge from suffering
oppositionStances.summary: Philo's catalogue of suffering challenges inference to a perfectly good and powerful cause of the world.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Philo, a speaker in Hume's Dialogues
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Eighteenth-century philosophical dialogue; speaker and author must remain distinct.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Scholars dispute the exact relation between Philo and Hume's final position.
oppositionStances.locator: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Parts X–XI; SEP Hume on Religion, problem-of-evil discussion

oppositionStances.title: Limits of the sufferer's standpoint
oppositionStances.summary: Job 38 responds to Job by stressing the limits of his standpoint rather than supplying a simple causal theodicy.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Divine speech as represented in Job
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Hebrew wisdom poetry in a historical English translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Job contains several competing speeches; one speech cannot be made the whole book's answer.

oppositionStances.title: Future redress
oppositionStances.summary: Demea proposes that present evils are rectified in another region or future existence.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Demea, a speaker in Hume's Dialogues
oppositionStances.historicalContext: A position staged and criticized within Hume's dialogue.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: This is Demea's reply, not an endorsed resolution by the whole dialogue.
oppositionStances.locator: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part X, Demea's future-state reply

oppositionStances.title: Suffering and judgments
oppositionStances.summary: Marcus Aurelius repeatedly reframes distress through judgments, agency, and participation in nature rather than a personal theodicy.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Second-century Roman Stoic notebook tradition.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Stoic providence and modern therapeutic readings should not be conflated.

oppositionStances.title: A path responding to suffering
oppositionStances.summary: The Dhammapada emphasizes impermanence, suffering, and a path of practice rather than an omnipotent creator's purposes.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Pali Buddhist verse collection in historical translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: This changes the question rather than logically refuting or defending classical theism.

oppositionStances.title: Natural causes without providence
oppositionStances.summary: Lucretius explains natural events through atoms and natural processes and attacks fear-producing providential explanations.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Roman Epicurean philosophical poem.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Ancient atomism differs from contemporary sciences and materialisms.
oppositionStances.locator: On the Nature of Things, Books V–VI, natural-cause arguments

oppositionStances.title: No compulsion in religion
oppositionStances.summary: Qur'an 2:256 states no compulsion in religion; interpretation, legal scope, and historical application require contextual study.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Seventh-century Arabic text presented through an academic corpus and historical translation.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The verse alone does not describe every Islamic legal or political practice.

oppositionStances.title: Imperial levy and forced conversion
oppositionStances.summary: The Ottoman devshirme periodically levied Christian boys, enslaved them, converted them, and trained them for state service.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Institutional practice developing from the fifteenth century; frequency and local implementation varied.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Benefits later attained by some recruits do not erase coercive intake; neither does the case describe all Ottoman conversion.
oppositionStances.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, pp. 271–278; Global Slavery, devshirme discussion

oppositionStances.title: Protected-status legal objection
oppositionStances.summary: Wittek frames devshirme as incompatible with sharia protections for Christian dhimmi subjects and notes Muslim objections.
oppositionStances.speakerOrCommunity: Muslim juristic conscience as reconstructed by Paul Wittek
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Modern scholarship on a historical legal controversy.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The included abstract does not name or reproduce every contemporary juristic voice.
oppositionStances.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, p. 271 and article extract

oppositionStances.title: Centralization and state formation
oppositionStances.summary: Comparative scholarship situates devshirme within military staffing, enslavement, elite formation, and centralization rather than reducing it to doctrine.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Modern state-formation analysis.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: Institutional and religious motives can coexist; the categories are not mutually exclusive.
oppositionStances.locator: Global Slavery in the Making of States and International Orders, Ottoman devshirme section

oppositionStances.title: Freedom and responsibility
oppositionStances.summary: Humanist Manifesto III ties dignity and ethical choice to freedom consonant with responsibility, opposing compelled affiliation as an ethical norm.
oppositionStances.historicalContext: Modern secular organizational statement.
oppositionStances.uncertainty: The manifesto does not discuss devshirme and is a modern ethical comparison, not a contemporary historical witness.

teachingConductCases.title: Christian ethical teaching and SPG plantation ownership
actorsAndInstitutions: Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG)

teachingEvidence.summary: Matthew 7:12 presents the Golden Rule; Matthew 22:39 presents love of neighbor. These are selected Christian teachings, not an exhaustive doctrine of slavery.

conductEvidence.summary: The SPG inherited two Barbados sugar plantations and about 300 enslaved Africans in 1710 and continued exploiting enslaved labor; the Church of England FAQ also documents branding with 'Society'.
conductEvidence.locator: Church of England Historic Links FAQ, Codrington section

justificationsAtTheTime.summary: Rev. Thomas Thompson defended slavery through the law of nations, biblical appeal, nature, necessity, and commerce. This is a named Anglican argument, not a uniform Christian or SPG theology.
justificationsAtTheTime.attributedTo: Rev. Thomas Thompson as documented in the cited study
justificationsAtTheTime.locator: The University of Cambridge in the Age of Atlantic Slavery, chapter 2, pp. 49–51

textsUsedToJustify.summary: Independent scholarship documents SPG-linked Anglican arguments that the Christian gospel did not interfere with civil property, with enslaved Africans treated as property, and a contemporary debate that invoked Christ's example and the authority of Scripture.
textsUsedToJustify.locator: The University of Cambridge in the Age of Atlantic Slavery, chapter 2, pp. 70–72
textsUsedToJustify.attributedTo: Thomas Sherlock, Thomas Thompson, Benjamin Hoadly, and other named Anglican clergy in the cited study

supportingReligiousVoices.summary: The SPG continued the plantation arrangement, while Rev. Thomas Thompson and named Anglican bishops argued that Christian conversion and the gospel did not dissolve enslavers' civil property claims.
supportingReligiousVoices.attributedTo: SPG governors, Thomas Thompson, Benjamin Hoadly, and Thomas Sherlock in the cited records
supportingReligiousVoices.locator: Cambridge Atlantic Slavery, chapter 2, pp. 49–51 and 70–72; Church of England FAQ, Codrington section

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Granville Sharp answered Thompson's proslavery case as a committed Christian, appealing to the gospel and universal benevolence while rejecting the claimed biblical and natural-law warrant.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: The University of Cambridge in the Age of Atlantic Slavery, chapter 2, pp. 49–51

nonreligiousMotives.summary: Sugar production, plantation revenue, labor control, and preservation of an endowment were economic and institutional motives alongside religious mission identity.
nonreligiousMotives.locator: Church of England Historic Links FAQ, Codrington plantation and endowment paragraphs

laterTheologicalInterpretations.summary: Later mission theology reads the Codrington legacy through scripture, liberation, repentance, and repair, while current Church research treats historic benefit from chattel enslavement as requiring accountability. These later readings do not erase institutional distinctions.
laterTheologicalInterpretations.attributedTo: Mission Studies scholarship and Church of England institutional review
laterTheologicalInterpretations.locator: Mission Studies 38.3 (2021), pp. 325–346; Church of England Historic Links FAQ, response programme paragraphs

modernScholarlyInterpretations.summary: Independent scholarship and the institutional archival review both document ownership, management, religious argument, and exploitation while keeping the SPG and later legally distinct institutions historically specific.
modernScholarlyInterpretations.attributedTo: Independent historians and Church Commissioners historical research
modernScholarlyInterpretations.locator: Cambridge Atlantic Slavery, chapter 2, pp. 40–75; Church of England Historic Links FAQ

teachingConductCases.evidenceStatus: High for ownership, labor exploitation, dates, and the cited scholarly reconstruction of named religious arguments; no single uniform SPG prooftext is asserted.
teachingConductCases.disputes: Responsibility and institutional continuity must distinguish the historic SPG, modern USPG, Church Commissioners, and the broader Church of England. Selected ethical verses do not establish how every historical Anglican interpreted slavery.
teachingConductCases.neutralityNote: Atlas juxtaposes a selected teaching and documented institutional conduct without declaring divine approval, collective guilt, or a theological verdict.

teachingConductCases.title: Buddhist non-harm teaching and Japanese Zen wartime support
actorsAndInstitutions: leaders and institutions within Japanese Zen

teachingEvidence.summary: Dhammapada verse 5 states that hatred does not cease by hatred; this is a selected Buddhist teaching, not proof that all Buddhist ethics are absolute pacifism.
The contemporary Sōtō organization explicitly presents non-violence and avoidance of warlike confrontation as Buddhist responsibilities.
teachingEvidence.locator: SOTOZEN SDG 16, non-violence and peace statement

conductEvidence.summary: Scholarship documents Zen leaders and institutions supporting Japanese imperial projects through propaganda, patriotic organizations, fundraising, ritual, and exhortation; the inspected article records specific Sōtō arguments and voices.
conductEvidence.locator: Ishikawa Rikizan (1998), pp. 88–93; Imperial-Way Zen, wartime-mobilization chapters

justificationsAtTheTime.summary: Wartime rhetoric drew on loyalty, service to the public, protection of the realm, national emergency, and interpretations connecting Zen discipline with imperial duty.
justificationsAtTheTime.locator: Imperial-Way Zen, chapters on imperial-way doctrine and protection of the realm

textsUsedToJustify.summary: Wartime Sōtō argument used the 'two truths' theory to subordinate Buddhist law to imperial law and presented loyalty to the emperor as an absolute religious obligation. The cited article preserves these as historically situated arguments.
textsUsedToJustify.attributedTo: Wartime Sōtō doctrinal argument documented by Ishikawa Rikizan

supportingReligiousVoices.summary: Named Zen leaders including Sawaki Kōdō and Nanjo Bun'yū linked Buddhist language, imperial loyalty, and wartime service; broader institutional mobilization included enlistment, fundraising, and ritual.
supportingReligiousVoices.attributedTo: Sawaki Kōdō, Nanjo Bun'yū, and other documented Zen leaders
supportingReligiousVoices.locator: Ishikawa Rikizan (1998), pp. 91–93; Imperial-Way Zen, named-leader chapters

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Sōtō priest Uchiyama Gudō opposed imperial authority and was later rehabilitated; the Sōtō apology literature treats his case as part of institutional reckoning.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: Ishikawa Rikizan (1998), Uchiyama Gudō discussion, pp. 74–87

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Makiguchi Tsunesaburō's conflict with wartime ideology provides a distinct Buddhist resistance case; it must not be generalized to all Sōka or Nichiren actors.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: We Alone Can Save Japan, Makiguchi and wartime-resistance sections

nonreligiousMotives.summary: Nationalism, state pressure, institutional survival, colonial expansion, military mobilization, and access to public legitimacy were non-doctrinal factors.
nonreligiousMotives.locator: Imperial-Way Zen, institutional-accommodation chapters; Ishikawa Rikizan (1998), pp. 88–105

laterTheologicalInterpretations.summary: The 1992 Sōtō statement acknowledged harm, loss of autonomy, and institutional responsibility; contemporary Sōtō materials articulate a no-war ethic.
laterTheologicalInterpretations.locator: Ishikawa Rikizan (1998), p. 105; SOTOZEN SDG 16 statement

modernScholarlyInterpretations.summary: Ives analyzes both active support and disputes about whether Zen doctrines, institutional accommodation, nationalism, or political coercion best explain wartime conduct.
modernScholarlyInterpretations.locator: Imperial-Way Zen, conclusion and responsibility analysis

teachingConductCases.evidenceStatus: High for documented institutional mobilization and later apology; medium for causal weight assigned to doctrine versus state, nationalist, and institutional pressures.
teachingConductCases.disputes: Scholars dispute the representativeness of individual figures, the interpretation of wartime rhetoric, and how much explanatory weight belongs to Zen ideas versus modern nationalism and coercive institutions.
teachingConductCases.neutralityNote: The case neither treats wartime conduct as Buddhist doctrine nor exempts documented religious institutions from historical analysis.

teachingConductCases.title: No-compulsion teaching and Ottoman devshirme

teachingEvidence.summary: Qur'an 2:256 states that there is no compulsion in religion. Its legal scope and historical applications have multiple interpretations.
Wittek summarizes the sharia principle that protected Christian subjects retained personal liberty and the right to practice their religion.
teachingEvidence.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, p. 271 and article extract

conductEvidence.summary: The devshirme was a periodic forced levy of Christian boys involving enslavement, conversion to Islam, and training for imperial military or administrative service.
conductEvidence.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, pp. 271–278; Global Slavery, Ottoman devshirme section

justificationsAtTheTime.summary: The included scholarship reconstructs service, military recruitment, household formation, and centralization as state rationales, but it does not establish a named contemporary religious justification. Atlas records that evidentiary limit instead of converting state practice into theology.
justificationsAtTheTime.locator: Global Slavery, Ottoman state-formation section; Wittek, pp. 271–278 (named religious defender not located)

textsUsedToJustify.summary: The included sources do not establish a single Qur'anic prooftext used by Ottoman administrators to authorize the levy. Atlas records the legal controversy instead of fabricating one.
textsUsedToJustify.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, pp. 271–278 (reviewed for, but does not establish, a Qur'anic prooftext)

supportingReligiousVoices.summary: No named contemporary religious scholar explicitly defending devshirme is established in the included evidence. State implementation demonstrates political support, not automatically a juristic endorsement.
supportingReligiousVoices.locator: Wittek, pp. 271–278 and Global Slavery devshirme section (reviewed for, but do not establish, a named juristic defender)

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Wittek reports that the levy appeared incompatible with the holy law's protection of Christian subjects, but the inspected material does not establish a named contemporary religious opponent. The legal conflict is evidence; a named voice remains a gap.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: Wittek, pp. 271–278 (legal conflict established; named contemporary religious opponent not established)

nonreligiousMotives.summary: Military labor, an imperial service elite, central control over frontier nobles, and state formation were major political and institutional motives.
nonreligiousMotives.locator: Global Slavery in the Making of States and International Orders, Ottoman devshirme section

laterTheologicalInterpretations.summary: Louis Massignon later described devshirme as a breach of the Prophet's compact protecting Christian subjects; Wittek develops the legal-historical problem without treating that judgment as a universal Muslim view.
laterTheologicalInterpretations.attributedTo: Louis Massignon as discussed by Paul Wittek
laterTheologicalInterpretations.locator: Wittek, Devshirme and Shari'a, p. 271, Massignon and protected-subject compact discussion

modernScholarlyInterpretations.summary: Recent comparative scholarship treats devshirme as coerced enslavement and conversion embedded in state formation while also noting later advancement available to some recruits.
modernScholarlyInterpretations.locator: Global Slavery in the Making of States and International Orders, Ottoman devshirme section

teachingConductCases.evidenceStatus: High for coercive levy, conversion, and service; medium for legal debates; the current evidence set lacks a named contemporary religious defender and records that gap.
teachingConductCases.disputes: Frequency, recruitment patterns, local agency, family strategies, and the experience of later elite advancement vary. None removes coercive intake, and none warrants generalizing devshirme to all Ottoman or Islamic conversion.
teachingConductCases.neutralityNote: The case compares a Qur'anic/legal norm with a state institution without declaring the institution representative of Islam as a whole.

teachingConductCases.title: Equal vision teaching and Vaikom road exclusion

teachingEvidence.summary: Bhagavad Gita 5:18 praises equal vision toward people of different social standing. This selected verse is not a complete account of Hindu varna or caste traditions.

conductEvidence.summary: Roads surrounding the Vaikom temple were closed to Ezhavas and other communities deemed untouchable, and authorities arrested nonviolent protesters seeking access.
conductEvidence.locator: Government of Kerala, Vaikom Satyagraha, campaign narrative pp. 1–22; Gandhi Heritage Portal chronology

justificationsAtTheTime.summary: Indam Thurutthi Devan Nilakanthan Nampyathiri defended inherited exclusion through Hindu Dharma Shastra, Shankarasmriti, tradition, karma, and reincarnation during the 1925 discussions. This is a named historical position, not a summary of Hinduism.
justificationsAtTheTime.locator: Government of Kerala, Vaikom Satyagraha, pp. 20–22

textsUsedToJustify.summary: The government history records an orthodox appeal to Hindu Dharma Shastra and Shankarasmriti during Gandhi's discussion with caste-Hindu leaders. The cited pages do not establish a single verse as the exclusive warrant.
textsUsedToJustify.locator: Government of Kerala, Vaikom Satyagraha, pp. 20–22

supportingReligiousVoices.summary: Indam Thurutthi Devan Nilakanthan Nampyathiri and other named attendees defended the inherited restriction and rejected Gandhi's proposed tests for change during the March 1925 discussion.
supportingReligiousVoices.attributedTo: Indam Thurutthi Devan Nilakanthan Nampyathiri and the documented caste-Hindu delegation
supportingReligiousVoices.locator: Government of Kerala, Vaikom Satyagraha, pp. 20–22; Gandhi Heritage Portal, March 1925 meeting

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Sri Narayana Guru supported the struggle against exclusion and met Gandhi during the campaign.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: Government of Kerala, Sree Narayana Guru campaign section; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Guru meeting

opposingReligiousVoices.summary: Gandhi joined prayer with protesters, negotiated with orthodox leaders and state figures, and argued for change within a religious and political reform framework.
opposingReligiousVoices.locator: Government of Kerala, Gandhi negotiations pp. 20–22; Gandhi Heritage Portal, March 1925 chronology

nonreligiousMotives.summary: Social status, control of public space, princely-state order, anti-caste mobilization, and Indian nationalist politics shaped the conflict alongside religious custom.
nonreligiousMotives.locator: Gandhian Nonviolent Struggle and Untouchability, campaign and settlement chapters; Government of Kerala campaign narrative

laterTheologicalInterpretations.summary: The included sources establish later reform memory around Vaikom and the 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation, but they do not establish one defined later theological interpretation with an inspected doctrinal source. Atlas records that limitation explicitly.
laterTheologicalInterpretations.locator: Gandhian Nonviolent Struggle and Untouchability, conclusion; Kerala and Gandhi public histories (reviewed for, but do not establish, one later doctrinal school)

modernScholarlyInterpretations.summary: Independent scholarship treats Vaikom as a nonviolent anti-untouchability campaign, disputes romanticized conversion narratives, and analyzes the campaign's controversial settlement alongside the public-history accounts.
modernScholarlyInterpretations.attributedTo: Mary Elizabeth King with government and Gandhi heritage histories retained as public-memory sources
modernScholarlyInterpretations.locator: Gandhian Nonviolent Struggle and Untouchability, campaign, settlement, and conclusion chapters

teachingConductCases.evidenceStatus: High for exclusion, protest dates, named reformers, and negotiated road opening; medium for motives and orthodox justifications summarized by commemorative sources.
teachingConductCases.disputes: The campaign's partial 1925 settlement, relationship to temple entry, roles of Gandhi and local reformers, and the weight of religious custom versus state and caste power require fuller independent scholarship.
teachingConductCases.neutralityNote: Atlas neither treats exclusion as the essence of Hindu doctrine nor hides the religious institutions and arguments present in the historical record.
